CausalChain: COL1A2 upregulation -> Enhanced integrin engagement -> Activation of FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK cascades -> Phosphorylation/modification of mRNA export regulators (XPO1, RNA-binding proteins) -> Selective enhanced export of oncogenic mRNAs -> Increased metastasis and angiogenesis -> Poorer liver neoplasm prognosis. (Parallel modulation via COL4A1/XPD-miR29a-3p and RORγ-driven ECM remodeling)
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in liver neoplasms, elevated COL1A2 levels serve a dual role: first, by remodeling the extracellular matrix to modulate tumor microenvironment in a manner analogous to the well-established roles of COL4A1 and RORγ-mediated ECM gene expression; and second, by triggering enhanced integrin engagement. This activation leads to concurrent stimulation of the FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK signaling pathways, which then phosphorylate mRNA export regulators, including XPO1 and specific RNA-binding proteins. Such post-translational modifications are proposed to selectively boost the nuclear export and subsequent translation of oncogenic mRNAs, promoting metastatic behavior and angiogenesis. Our strategy employs CRISPR-based gene editing to create precise perturbations at the COL1A2 locus and kinetic mapping of kinase activities through quantitative phosphoproteomics, supplemented with RNA immunoprecipitation assays to test mRNA export selectivity. This integrated approach will decipher the nuanced interplay between extracellular cues and nuclear export dynamics in liver cancer and may illuminate new therapeutic targets.
Abstract: In liver neoplasms, we posit that elevated COL1A2 expression contributes to tumor progression via a dual mechanism that integrates both conventional ECM remodeling and a novel intracellular signaling cascade. Our revised hypothesis proposes that COL1A2 upregulation not only alters the extracellular matrix but also enhances integrin engagement, leading to the activation of FAK/PI3K-AKT and MAPK kinase cascades. These activated kinases phosphorylate key mRNA export regulators, such as XPO1 and specific RNA-binding proteins. This phosphorylation event is hypothesized to selectively promote the export and translation of oncogenic mRNAs, thereby driving metastasis and angiogenesis. In harmony with established regulatory pathways—such as the COL4A1 regulation via the XPD–miR-29a-3p axis and RORγ-mediated ECM gene expression—we propose that COL1A2-mediated signaling acts in concert with these mechanisms to exacerbate liver cancer progression. The use of contemporary technologies, including CRISPR-based gene editing, quantitative phosphoproteomics, and RNA immunoprecipitation assays, will allow us to systematically dissect and validate each step in this complex, multi-layered signaling cascade.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis focused exclusively on a cascade from COL1A2-mediated ECM remodeling to integrin activation, kinase signaling, and modulation of mRNA export regulators leading to metastasis. The revised hypothesis retains the same causal chain but explicitly acknowledges alternative, well-established pathways (e.g., COL4A1 via the XPD–miR29a-3p regulatory axis and RORγ-driven ECM remodeling) that contribute to metastatic progression in liver neoplasms. Moreover, the new version refines the specificity of the mechanism by addressing how phosphorylation events might confer selective export of oncogenic mRNAs and outlines a detailed experimental framework using cutting-edge techniques such as CRISPR, quantitative phosphoproteomics, and RNA immunoprecipitation. This not only aligns better with current observations from related studies but also enhances the practical implementability and scientific robustness of the hypothesis.
